title: Records, structs and enums
summary: Pick the right kind of type: named choices, small values, and data that compares by content.

steps.title: Enums: a fixed set of choices
body: An order's status could be a string. Then one day someone types `"shiped"` and the compiler says nothing.
An **enum** is a type whose only possible values are the names you list:
enum OrderStatus { Pending, Paid, Shipped, Cancelled }
- A typo such as `OrderStatus.Shiped` is a compile error.
- Your editor can list every valid choice.
- Underneath, each name is a number counting from 0. You rarely need it, but a cast shows it.
Use an enum whenever a value is *one of a small known list*: a status, a priority, a day of the week.

steps.prompt: Declare a claim status, set it, and test it.
steps.explain: Enum values are reached through the type name with a dot, and compared with `==` like numbers.

steps.title: Structs: values, not references
body: A class variable holds a reference, so two variables can share one object. A **struct** is the opposite: the variable holds the data itself, and assigning it makes a **copy**.
Size b = a;        // a full copy
`int`, `decimal`, `bool` and every enum are value types too. That is why `int y = x;` has always given you an independent copy.

Reach for a struct only when the thing is **small and behaves like a single value**: a size, a coordinate, an amount of money. For anything with identity or a lifetime, such as a customer or an account, use a class.

steps.prompt: The **only** difference between these two types is the keyword. What does the program print?
steps.explain: `s2` is a copy, so `s1` never changes. `c2` is a second reference to the same object, so `c1` sees the 5.

steps.title: Records: data that compares by content
body: Two class objects are equal only if they are the **same object**. For pure data that is rarely what you mean: £5 is £5.
A **record** is a class built for data. One line gives you a constructor, read-only properties, equality by content and a readable `ToString`.
- The names in the parentheses become `init`-only properties, so a record cannot be changed after it is made.
- `==` compares every property. This is called **value equality**.
- You can still add methods and computed properties inside `{ }` when you need them.
Use a record for things that are *just their data*: a price, an address, a line in a transaction log.

steps.prompt: Same data, class versus record. What does this print?
steps.explain: Two class objects are two different objects, whatever they contain. Two records with the same contents are equal. The record also prints its own contents.

steps.title: Focus blocks as records
prompt: Write a record for one block of `sk focus`. Your `Sk.FormatMinutes(minutes)` from First steps is ready to call.
`record Block(string Kind, int Minutes)` with a computed property `string Label` that returns `"<Kind> <formatted minutes>"`.
`new Block("focus", 25).Label` is `"focus 0h 25m"`. Two blocks with the same values are equal, and `with` makes a changed copy.
template: var dojoB = new Block("focus", 25);
Dojo.Eq("Label", "focus 0h 25m", dojoB.Label);
Dojo.Eq("same values are equal", true, dojoB == new Block("focus", 25));
Dojo.Eq("different values are not", false, dojoB == new Block("break", 25));
var dojoLong = dojoB with { Minutes = 50 };
Dojo.Eq("with makes a changed copy", "focus 0h 50m", dojoLong.Label);
Dojo.Eq("the original is unchanged", 25, dojoB.Minutes);
{{CODE}}
static partial class Sk
internal static string FormatMinutes(int minutes)
string result = "";
int hours = minutes / 60;
int rest = minutes % 60;
result = $"{hours}h {rest:00}m";
return result;
hints: Give the record a body: `record Block(string Kind, int Minutes) { ... }`.

steps.title: Changing a record: with
body: Records cannot be modified, so how does a claim become approved? You make a **new** record that copies the old one and changes what you name. That is a `with` expression.
var approved = submitted with { Status = ClaimStatus.Approved };
The original is untouched. This sounds wasteful and turns out to be a relief: a value you were handed can never change behind your back, so there is a whole class of bug you stop looking for.
Inside a record's own method, `this with { ... }` does the same thing.

steps.prompt: When you write `b = a;`, does `b` get its own copy, or a reference to the same object?
steps.explain: A record is a class underneath, so it is a reference type. It only *compares* by value. Because it cannot be changed, sharing one is harmless.

steps.title: Flags: several choices at once
body: A normal enum holds **one** choice. Sometimes you need a combination: a user may read *and* write.
Mark the enum `[Flags]` and give each value its own power of two. Then `|` combines them and `HasFlag` tests for one.
enum Permissions { None = 0, Read = 1, Write = 2, Delete = 4 }
The values are 1, 2, 4, 8 so that every combination adds up to a different number. You will not write many of these, but you will meet them in the .NET libraries.

code: enum Permissions { None = 0, Read = 1, Write = 2, Delete = 4 }
steps.explain: `Read` is 1 and `Delete` is 4, so together they are 5. `[Flags]` makes `WriteLine` list the names instead of printing the number.

steps.title: Sidekick piece: time entries and statuses
prompt: **Sidekick piece.** Every time you stop a timer, Sidekick writes down a **time entry**: which task, from when, until when. Your standup and weekly reports are built from these. Write three types.
**1.** `enum Status { Todo, Doing, Blocked, Done }`, in that order.
**2.** `record TimeEntry(int TaskId, DateTime Start, DateTime End)` with two computed properties:
- `int Minutes`: the whole minutes from `Start` to `End`;
**3.** `static class StatusRules` with `static bool CanMove(Status from, Status to)`. Allowed moves:
Everything else, including staying put and anything out of `Done`, is `false`. A `switch` on the tuple `(from, to)` with `or` patterns says it in a few lines.
starter: enum Status { Todo, Doing, Blocked, Done }
record TimeEntry(int TaskId, DateTime Start, DateTime End);
public static bool CanMove(Status from, Status to)
solution: enum Status { Todo, Doing, Blocked, Done }
record TimeEntry(int TaskId, DateTime Start, DateTime End)
public static bool CanMove(Status from, Status to) => (from, to) switch
(Status.Doing, Status.Todo or Status.Blocked or Status.Done) => true,
template: var dojoE = new TimeEntry(3, new DateTime(2026, 11, 24, 9, 0, 0), new DateTime(2026, 11, 24, 10, 30, 0));
Dojo.Eq("TaskId", 3, dojoE.TaskId);
Dojo.Eq("Minutes", 90, dojoE.Minutes);
Dojo.Eq("Day", new DateOnly(2026, 11, 24), dojoE.Day);
Dojo.Eq("59 seconds are 0 minutes", 0, new TimeEntry(1, new DateTime(2026, 11, 24, 9, 0, 0), new DateTime(2026, 11, 24, 9, 0, 59)).Minutes);
Dojo.Eq("entries with the same values are equal", true, dojoE == new TimeEntry(3, new DateTime(2026, 11, 24, 9, 0, 0), new DateTime(2026, 11, 24, 10, 30, 0)));
Dojo.Eq("with moves the end", 120, (dojoE with { End = new DateTime(2026, 11, 24, 11, 0, 0) }).Minutes);
Dojo.Eq("the statuses, in order", "Todo,Doing,Blocked,Done", string.Join(",", Enum.GetNames<Status>()));
Dojo.Eq("Todo to Doing", true, StatusRules.CanMove(Status.Todo, Status.Doing));
Dojo.Eq("Todo to Done", true, StatusRules.CanMove(Status.Todo, Status.Done));
Dojo.Eq("Todo to Blocked is not allowed", false, StatusRules.CanMove(Status.Todo, Status.Blocked));
Dojo.Eq("Doing to Blocked", true, StatusRules.CanMove(Status.Doing, Status.Blocked));
Dojo.Eq("Doing back to Todo", true, StatusRules.CanMove(Status.Doing, Status.Todo));
Dojo.Eq("Blocked to Doing", true, StatusRules.CanMove(Status.Blocked, Status.Doing));
Dojo.Eq("Blocked to Done is not allowed", false, StatusRules.CanMove(Status.Blocked, Status.Done));
Dojo.Eq("nothing leaves Done", false, StatusRules.CanMove(Status.Done, Status.Todo));
Dojo.Eq("staying put is not a move", false, StatusRules.CanMove(Status.Todo, Status.Todo));
{{CODE}}
hints: Inside the record's body: `public int Minutes => (int)(End - Start).TotalMinutes;` and `public DateOnly Day => DateOnly.FromDateTime(Start);`.
One arm per row of the table, e.g. `(Status.Todo, Status.Doing or Status.Done) => true,`, and `_ => false` last.
steps.explain: A record is the right shape for an entry: it is data, two equal entries are the same entry, and it never changes after it is written. The enum makes impossible statuses impossible to type.
